pitchHistory.title: The Woman Who Remembered Everything: How Henrietta Lacks's Cells Outlived Every Doctor Who Took Them
pitchHistory.summary: In February 1951, a 31-year-old Black tobacco farmer from Clover, Virginia walked into Johns Hopkins Hospital complaining of unusual bleeding — and left behind something that would become one of the most consequential biological materials in human history, without ever being asked. This is the story not of HeLa cells the scientific landmark, but of Henrietta Lacks the person: her voice, her laughter, her red-painted toenails on the autopsy table, and what it means that her involuntary gift underpins the polio vaccine, cancer research, and COVID-19 therapeutics while her grandchildren struggled to afford health insurance. The story sits at the crossroads of race, medicine, memory, and ownership — but it earns its weight through one woman's particular, irreplaceable life.

pitchHistory.title: The Man Who Said No at the Bottom of the Ocean
pitchHistory.summary: In October 1962, a Soviet submarine sealed beneath the Atlantic — cut off from Moscow, depth-charged by American destroyers, its crew convinced World War III had already begun — came within one vote of launching a nuclear torpedo. The man who cast the deciding 'no' was a 34-year-old officer named Vasili Arkhipov, and almost no one has heard his name. This post tells the story of the most consequential dissent in human history, made in darkness, under pressure, by someone who had no way of knowing whether he was saving the world or simply delaying its end.

However, the post generally handles uncertainty well, using qualifiers like 'reportedly,' 'appears to have argued,' and 'No one knows exactly what Arkhipov said.'

pitchHistory.title: The Man Who Recorded the Truth and Then Disappeared: Valery Legasov's Tapes
pitchHistory.summary: On April 27, 1988 — exactly two years and one day after Reactor No. 4 exploded at Chernobyl — Soviet chemist Valery Legasov took his own life. But before he did, he recorded five cassette tapes: a meticulous, damning account of everything the Soviet scientific establishment had lied about, suppressed, and ignored. With the 40th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster arriving on April 26, 2026, this is the moment to tell Legasov's story not through the HBO dramatization that simplified him, but as it actually happened — a man caught between institutional loyalty and an unbearable debt to the truth, who chose the only form of testimony left to him.
pitchHistory.editorNotes: Word count is approximately 1,300 words (~6.5 min read), within the target range but at the upper end.; Several historical claims are presented as fact without cited sources — e.g., the specific detail that the graphite-tip design flaw was 'known to Soviet physicists since the 1970s,' the claim that Legasov was passed over for Academy membership as institutional rebuke for his Vienna openness, and the assertion that he 'left that part out' at Vienna. While these claims are broadly consistent with the historical record and widely reported, the post does not cite or link to any sources. Recommend adding references or brief attribution (e.g., to published transcripts of the tapes, Zhores Medvedev's work, or other Chernobyl scholarship) to strengthen credibility.; Some details involve minor narrative embellishment or inference presented as established fact — e.g., 'dead for several hours before anyone thought to look for the tapes,' 'stacked with the quiet deliberateness of a man who had decided...' These read as literary reconstruction rather than documented fact. Consider flagging these as the author's narrative interpretation.
